newsitem.title: GERMANY: European equities fired up by early Wall St rally.
newsitem.headline: European equities fired up by early Wall St rally.

text.p: Europe's stock market bulls shook off single currency anxieties to hit new record highs on Friday, with sentiment boosted by early rises on Wall Street and with little evidence of vertigo at these new dizzy heights.

Analysts still see substantial upside in Europe's equity markets, but potential stumbling blocks remain the future of European economic and monetary union (EMU), possible interest rate rises or a correction on Wall Street.

The Dow Jones Industrial index of U.S. stocks continued its greatest bull run ever on Friday, rising one percent in early trade, boosting sentiment across Europe, and highlighting yet again just how dependent Europe's bourses are on Wall Street.

Hopes of a ratification of a European stability pact at next week's EU summit in Amsterdam also lifted spirits, after recent worries that the pact, aimed at ensuring fiscal discipline among currency union members after the euro is adopted after January 1, 1999, may fall at the last hurdle.

Key to these fears were worries that the newly-elected French government might try to stymie the stability pact. But French market players said calls by the Socialist government for an "employment charter" attached to the pact were not such a bad idea, as unemployment was destabilising.

"The fundamentals are still very strong, with low inflation, momentum in the overall economy and a good earnings outlook," a Paris broker said. Dealers said a level of 3,000 points on the CAC index was possible by year end.

Investors who did not buy when the CAC index fell to 2,500 in the spring on election uncertainty were now looking to get into the Paris market, which has lagged other European bourses by three or four percent in recent weeks, the broker said.
The CAC 40 index was up one percent at 2,788.42 points in late trade, just off record highs of 2,805.37 points.

Comments late on Thursday by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer signalling that sustainability, not precise figures, were of primary importance for the success of EMU, helped euro optimism on German markets.

"There is more confidence out there that the euro will come on time, even if it's weaker than expected, so people now expect that money will keep coming into Europe after currency union," Jochen Waiblinger, assistant vice president of the Institutional Investors department at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
Germany's IBIS DAX electronic index has been breaking records on an almost daily basis, hitting an all-time high of 3,760.98 points earlier in the day.
One bank said in a report that the forecast for the DAX reaching 3,800 points looks "increasingly conservative".
Perhaps typically, Britain's stock market has paid little heed to turmoil in continental Europe sparked by EMU worries.
Analysts said the outlook for UK shares was more dependent on the July 2 budget and prospects for interest rates through the rest of the year, alongside developments on Wall Street.

"The EMU situation doesn't affect the FTSE one way or another, it is only relevant when EMU gets the go-ahead and when the pound is going to join," said Joe Rooney, strategist at investment bank Lehman Brothers in London. The FTSE was up 16.2 points at 4,773.6 points in late trade, not far off a high of 4,796.
These huge gains have prompted fears that Europe's markets may be overextended, creating a "bubble" just waiting to burst.
Analysts said a background of moderate growth in Europe, low inflation and interest rates and continent-wide corporate restructuring programmes was reassuring.
Institutional investors remain bullish on European equity markets and this influx of funds is keeping liquidity buoyant.

One possible downside is that with European indices trading at such highs, some stocks are overvalued, which means a bout of profit-taking is possible in the mid-term, but with Wall Street rallying, no-one can afford to be out of Europe now.
* AEX index in Amsterdam at 848.02 points, just off record at 848.29 points, seen hitting 850 initially, then 875 points.
* SMI at 5,396.1, just off record at 5,396.5.
* Spain's IBEX-35 at 6,704.60 points, within sight of record at 6,743.33 points.
